quizzes.title: Module Intro: Before You Begin
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRO
Module Intro: Before You Begin
3 questions · survey · one attempt
Instructions

Welcome to this module. This short survey is not graded for correctness. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting.

questions.text: Why might a powerful nation fail to win a war even when it has stronger weapons and more soldiers? Give your best answer now. You will come back to this question at the end of the module.

This module has these goals. Read them, then choose one answer.

  • Explain why the United States became involved in Vietnam, including the domino theory.
  • Describe the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and what it did and did not say.
  • Explain Johnson's decisions of 1965 and the strategy of attrition.
  • Describe the Tet Offensive and the credibility gap.
  • Describe the student movement, the counterculture, and the other movements of the 1960s.
  • Explain what Nixon meant by the silent majority, and why 1968 was a breaking point.

answers.text: I have read the goals and I understand what this module asks of me.
I have read the goals, but I have a question about one of them.

questions.text: Some assignments in this course allow you to work with classmates. How do you plan to work this module?

answers.text: I would like to work with a group when that is an option.
I would rather work on my own.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Vietnam and the Turbulent Sixties
quizzes.description:
READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Vietnam and the Turbulent Sixties
8 questions · 8 points · one attempt
Before you start

Answer each question using what you learned in this week's two lessons. You may look back at them, but the answers are not stated word for word. You will need to put facts together.

questions.text: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution passed the Senate 88 to 2 and the House 416 to 0, yet it was not a declaration of war. What problem does this raise for a republic?

answers.text: The Senate had no power to vote on military matters.
The president had asked for a declaration of war, and Congress refused.
Congress handed the president wide power in one quick vote, with no limit on the size or length of any fighting.
The resolution allowed fighting only in the Gulf of Tonkin.

questions.text: In 1964, Johnson won in part by promising not to send American boys to fight an Asian war. In 1965 he sent 125,000 men. Which of his concerns helps explain why he did not put the decision to Congress or ask the nation for sacrifice?

answers.text: He feared a great debate over the war might endanger the Great Society and frighten China into the war.
He had been told that the war would be over by Christmas.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff had ordered him to keep it secret.
The Constitution gave the Senate no part in the matter.

questions.text: American commanders measured success by "body count." Why did a rising body count not mean that the United States was winning?

answers.text: The enemy never lost any fighters.
Congress refused to count the dead.
Most of the enemy's losses were American.
The enemy only had to avoid losing and outlast American patience, and men and supplies kept coming down the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

questions.text: The Tet Offensive was a military defeat for the communists, yet it was a political disaster for Johnson. What best explains this?

answers.text: The communists captured the whole of South Vietnam.
Americans had been told the war was being won, and then they saw the fighting at the embassy in Saigon on television.
Congress used the offensive to end the draft.
The offensive showed that the Gulf of Tonkin attack had never happened.

questions.text: Which pair of facts best supports the criticism that Johnson did not ask the whole nation to share the burden of the war?

answers.text: He bombed the north, and he met with advisers.
Soldiers were all volunteers, and the war was short.
Congress declared war, and taxes were raised sharply.
He did not ask Congress or the nation to make sacrifices, and college students and others could often avoid the draft.

questions.text: In 1969, Nixon asked for the support of the "silent majority." Which person best fits what he meant?

answers.text: A factory worker who paid taxes, supported the country, and never marched in a protest.
A student who led a sit-in at Berkeley.
A visitor to Haight-Ashbury in the Summer of 1967.
A student who marched on the Pentagon.

questions.text: After riots in Watts, Newark, and Detroit, a commission blamed white racism and poverty. How did many white Americans respond?

answers.text: They called for an end to the draft.
With fear and anger, and some began to doubt whether the Great Society was working.
They joined the Black Power movement.
They asked Congress to repeal the Civil Rights Act.

questions.text: Walter Cronkite told his audience that the war looked like a stalemate. Why was that statement so damaging to the government?

answers.text: Cronkite had been a soldier in Vietnam.
Cronkite was running for president.
Only months earlier, General Westmoreland had said that the enemy was losing and the end was in sight.
Cronkite said that North Vietnam had won the war.

quizzes.title: Module Outro: Looking Back
quizzes.description:
MODULE OUTRO
Module Outro: Looking Back
5 questions · survey · one attempt
Instructions

You have finished this module. Please answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see how the class is doing.

questions.text: Look back at the question from the start of the module. Why might a powerful nation fail to win a war even when it has stronger weapons and more soldiers? Give your answer now, using at least one fact from this module. You may say if your thinking has changed.
How confident do you feel about the material in this module?

answers.text: Very confident. I could explain it to someone else.
Fairly confident. I understand most of it.
Somewhat unsure. I understand parts of it.
Not confident. I need help.

questions.text: What is still unclear to you? Name a person, event, or idea. If nothing is unclear, write "nothing."
Which of these did the people in this module most need, whether they had it or not?

answers.text: Courage
Courtesy
Honesty
Perseverance
Self-government
Service
Responsibility

questions.text: Pick one person from this module (Johnson, Westmoreland, Nixon, Betty Friedan, Cesar Chavez, or someone else) and explain, in two or three sentences, how that virtue showed up in what they did, or how its absence did.

discussions.title: Discussion: Vietnam: Could America Have Won?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Discussion: Vietnam: Could America Have Won?
10 points · threaded discussion
Before you start

Open the lessons "Vietnam: From Advisers to Stalemate" and "The Counterculture and the Movements". Use My Notebook on those pages to gather your notes and marks, then come back here to post.

The question

The United States sent more than half a million troops to Vietnam and had far more firepower than its enemy, yet the war ended in a stalemate and a withdrawal. Could America have won? Before you answer, decide what "won" would have meant.

Your post

Your post (about 100 to 150 words):

  1. Take a clear position: yes, no, or only under conditions you name.
  2. Give one specific piece of evidence from the lesson "Vietnam: From Advisers to Stalemate" or the source The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution that supports you.
  3. Name one fact that cuts against your position, and explain why you still hold it.
Your reply

Your reply (about 50 to 75 words): Respond to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with something they did not use. If not, say respectfully where their reasoning falls short.

Before you post

Post first, then reply. You will not see your classmates' posts until you have posted.

Rubric
Post and reply
10.0 pts		10.0 pts Substantive
Clear position, specific evidence from the week, names a counterpoint, and the reply engages a classmate's actual reasoning		6.0 pts Thin
Position stated but evidence vague, no counterpoint, or the reply only says "I agree"		0.0 pts Missing
No post, or no reply
